title: Distance-rewired connectome nulls were liberal in 191 IBL mouse regions; a calibrated test kept wiring links for task encoding and thalamic bursts, not for spike waveform shape
abstract: Question: does the specific axonal wiring of a mouse brain region predict its physiology beyond geometry and cell-type composition? Data: 63,086 good units in 191 regions (IBL Brain-Wide Map 2026_Q2), Knox 2019 connectome, Allen CCF centroids and MERFISH supertype composition (Allen Brain Cell Atlas). We regressed 18 regional features (9 spike-physiology, 4 technical, 5 task-decoding) on their input-weighted neighbour mean, with distance, co-recording, division and transcriptome controls. The planned test against connectomes rewired within distance deciles passed (pooled physiology beta 0.27, p = 0.001; technical control p = 0.65). But on synthetic maps with no wiring dependence, this null gave 50-67% false positives for distance-smooth maps (7-28% with finer strata). A Gaussian-process surrogate null (distance, transcriptome and division covariance) had a 5.0% false-positive rate on 300 synthetic maps. With it, all 5 task variables followed specific wiring (mean beta 0.48 vs null 0.05, p = 0.001), spike physiology did so weakly (0.21 vs 0.12, p = 0.012; no single feature after Holm correction; waveform shape had no signal), and technical features did not (p = 0.41). Transcriptomic similarity carried a median 55% of the variance of physiology features. The thalamic link between isocortical input share and burst fraction (rho 0.74, 27 nuclei) exceeded rewired connectomes (null mean 0.36, p = 0.001) and Gaussian-process surrogate maps (p = 0.001). Limitations: correlational region averages; the surrogate null covers only the structure that it models.

False-positive rate at p < 0.05 on synthetic region maps that do not depend on wiring. Rewiring within distance bins is liberal; the Gaussian-process surrogate null is near 5%.
